report:
## Report

The evidence strongly supports, not refutes, the claim that hands-only (compression-only) bystander CPR improves survival compared with no bystander CPR after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA).

Large observational cohorts and registries consistently show this benefit. A Japanese nationwide population-based study found survival to discharge was 5.2% with no bystander CPR, 7.8% with conventional CPR, and 13.3% with compression-only CPR—both CPR types outperforming no CPR (https://www.hmpgloballearningnetwork.com/site/emsworld/article/10319099/literature-review-compression-only-cpr-oohca-bystanders). Data from the U.S. Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES), covering nearly 195,000 witnessed arrests, similarly demonstrates that any bystander CPR—including hands-only—is associated with better survival than none, with benefit diminishing as time to CPR initiation increases (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0300957225000784).

Regarding whether hands-only is as good as, or better than, conventional CPR with rescue breaths (a separate question from the "any CPR vs none" comparison), the American Heart Association's scientific statement concluded adults receiving hands-only or conventional CPR have similar survival chances (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380), and this equivalence has been echoed in more recent meta-analyses, some even suggesting a slight advantage for compression-only CPR (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34622436/).

**Conclusion:** The claim is well-supported by observational registry data and endorsed by the AHA; it is not false. Hands-only CPR shows clear survival benefit over no bystander CPR, and performs comparably to (sometimes better than) conventional CPR with breaths, especially for adult, non-drowning/non-pediatric arrests. No credible evidence found contradicts this consensus.
